content:
Who decided that owners cannot return to Wang Fuk Court?

Multiple owners raised the issue during the Q&A session. At least five questioners challenged Hop On, asking which government department had decided to bar them from returning and what legal basis underpinned the cordon. Hop On initially sidestepped the question four times, saying Wang Fuk Court was still sealed off and that it was beyond the manager's authority to arrange access, and advised owners to contact their dedicated social worker if needed — prompting an outcry among owners at several venues.

Hop On does not know the legal basis for the cordon

Solicitor Leung Ping-chiu eventually replied that Hop On did not know under what legal basis the authorities had sealed off the estate and it would be inappropriate for them to explain on the government's behalf, lest they misrepresent its considerations. On the survey reports for the remaining seven blocks of Wang Fuk Court — another issue of widespread concern — Hop On said typhoon and rainy seasons were approaching, and the reports might be released once the authorities completed their inspections. Hop On added that after taking legal advice, it considered the request to exceed its responsibilities as manager.

Owners concerned the government is using donations to reclaim titles — can it save compensation by not rebuilding?

The government has stated it will not rebuild on the original site. At the meeting, several owners questioned whether this meant the HK$2 billion "fire insurance" payout, calculated on the cost of restoring the building structure, would not be honoured: "Is the government using donations to take back the titles and not rebuild so that China Taiping can save on compensation?" China Taiping Insurance (Hong Kong) representative Ms Lau said that once policy liability is established, the company would pay out according to the policy terms regardless of whether repair or rebuilding takes place, and that acquisition would not affect policy liability or the calculation of the amount. However, Ms Lau added that the specific policy and legal liability could only be further assessed after the independent committee and relevant government departments had completed their investigations and announced the results.

Estimated repair cost for Wang Chi House is HK$30 million

Hop On also reported on the situation at Wang Chi House, which was not damaged. It had previously said that repairing Wang Chi House would cost at least HK$30 million and take at least nine months, involving re-laying external walls and restoring electrical systems. Today it updated the total to about HK$32 million, with a construction period of three to nine months. Invited solicitor Leung Ping-chiu noted that Wang Chi House forms part of the entire estate under the Deed of Mutual Covenant, and separating it out would require substantial amendments to the DMC with the consent of all owners — a complicated and costly procedure.

Owners question why Hop On did not hold a general meeting within the statutory deadline on the grounds that contacting owners takes time, yet managed to disburse URA subsidy cheques on its behalf earlier this year — "I want to ask, what's so difficult that you can't find us owners to hold a meeting?" Meeting chair Chan Wai-kwong, Hop On's property services director, did not give a direct answer, saying it was a venue issue — it was hard to find a space that could accommodate a thousand residents, and the Home Affairs Department eventually had to provide a venue for the meeting to proceed. One owner slammed the explanation as unreasonable: "Hong Kong has so many mega events, you can easily stage a show for tens of thousands in one venue, and you're telling me you can't find a place for our 2,000 people? That's really hard to swallow — I hope you won't use that as an excuse again."

"It's totally not what we wanted"

Ms Kwan, who left the meeting early and spoke to the media again afterwards, said the owners' meeting had failed to address her concerns: "The ball just gets kicked around — it's totally not what we wanted." China Taiping said the insurance payout would have to wait for the independent committee's report and investigations by relevant departments. Ms Kwan said the acquisition deadline of 31 August made waiting for compensation pointless: "All the answers will only come after 31 August. By then, if we've sold, none of it will concern us anymore." She had submitted a letter of intent but had not yet signed the sale and purchase agreement. After attending the meeting, she felt owners should first "insist on not selling" and only sell after 31 August, once there were answers. "If you sign before 31 August, all the reports will only come out afterwards, and we won't be owners anymore — what does it have to do with us?"

Regarding the next owners' meeting, Ms Kwan said if it were held in two months and she had signed, she would no longer be an owner and would have no right to attend. Asked why it seemed the next meeting would be scheduled two months later, she retorted: "Then help me ask (Hop On) why two months later? Why does the (independent committee) only need to release its report in two months (editor's note: should be October)?"

Wang Tai House resident Kitty held similar views, saying the meeting had not answered her questions. The biggest concern, she noted, was the insurance payout: "The insurance assessment won't come until September (editor's note: China Taiping said it has to wait for the independent committee's report and investigations by relevant departments) — by September, we'll have sold in August, so when the report comes out, the insurance won't concern us anymore!" She also criticised that the next owners' meeting might not be held for another two months: "Two months later, I've sold my flat — what's the point of holding a meeting?" On Hop On's response about whether owners could attend after selling, Kitty dismissed it as "playing tai chi": "They're just saying, once you've sold, it's none of your business." She also worried the government might legislate to acquire the titles: "If I don't sell my title to you, do I have to go to jail? Solve my problem and I'll sell to you." Kitty said she hoped to find a satisfactory flat and criticised the resettlement units for being much smaller than Wang Fuk Court. "They aren't big enough to live in, and if you compensate me based on the size, it won't be enough to buy a bigger one!" She said she would not sign the sale and purchase agreement for now: "It's been said that once you sign, nothing concerns you, and you won't have a share when rehousing happens — we hope for a third rehousing."

Mr Chan, who in the morning accused Hop On of being a government puppet, said he had already learnt everything he needed to know. "After asking so many questions, they all went round in circles — they couldn't answer." For example, he had asked whether the HK$2 billion compensation for the building's damage in the natural disaster was not payable if there were no plans to rebuild or repair. "The insurance company was just beating about the bush, acting as if they don't understand Chinese — no proper answer, completely off the point." Mr Chan was also concerned about the legal aspects of claiming compensation. He said Hop On had explained the legal procedure: "They said it could be a very lengthy process, requiring a legal team, and if we sue and lose, owners might have to share the legal fees."

He described the slides shown by Hop On as negative and turned the question back on them: should a legal team or legal representative, whose duty is to safeguard clients' interests, first estimate the chances of winning before litigation and, if successful, apply to the court for the other side to pay legal costs? "The lawyer did confirm this, but it's only something they'd say if we asked — the more positive aspects only come out when we push them." Mr Chan felt residents were dissatisfied with the meeting arrangements, starting with splitting everyone into different venues. "I don't believe Hong Kong has nowhere that can fit 2,000 flats — two representatives per household means 4,000 people. A concert at Kai Tak has 50,000!" He believed even the Hong Kong Stadium would work, and air conditioning was not essential.

Mr Chan also noted that owners had received calls or authorised representative information the previous day, and accused Hop On of "moving the goalposts" when it briefly changed the rule to allow only one representative per household. He believed the multiple venues had caused great controversy. "Under our pressure, or when the argument got so heated we could have torn down the building, they gave in — but you are obstructing us. I always say Hop On should help us, not hinder us." Asked whether he felt Hop On had helped them, he replied: "Help us? Help us with what? I don't see how they've helped us at all." As for the date of the next owners' meeting, Mr Chan said bluntly: "A person of normal thinking wouldn't expect a meeting to be held before 31 August." He explained that some residents had asked for another meeting a week before 31 August, but Hop On again cited venue difficulties, saying it was hard to arrange. He had no expectations. He said he had not yet signed the sale and purchase agreement and would "see how it goes", likening the current situation to a lucky dip — nothing was guaranteed, and there was no big incentive to sell the flat.
